title: A Fair Land and a New Name
overview: The book of Ezekiel ends with a vision of the land shared out equally among Israel's tribes, with God's temple at the center and a city whose name declares that the LORD lives there.

parts.label: Seven tribes in the north (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Each tribe gets an equal strip of land running east to west, drawn with little regard for real hills and valleys, which many scholars read as an idealized picture of fairness. Even tribes that had once lived east of the Jordan River are now brought inside the land with everyone else.

parts.label: The holy district (vv. 8-14)
parts.note: A strip set apart for God sits in the middle, with the temple at its center and land for the priests and for the Levites, their helpers. The priests descended from Zadok receive the inner part because they stayed faithful, and none of this land may ever be sold, because it belongs to the LORD.

parts.label: The city and the prince (vv. 15-22)
parts.note: The rest of this central square holds an ordinary city with pasture and farms worked by people from every tribe, so the city belongs to the whole nation. The land on either side goes to the prince, which seems meant to stop rulers from seizing other people's land, something Ezekiel condemned earlier.

parts.label: Five tribes in the south (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad fill the southern strips, ending at a border running down to the desert and the Mediterranean Sea. The land is called an inheritance, family property meant to pass down the generations and not be lost.

parts.label: Twelve gates for twelve tribes (vv. 30-34)
parts.note: The square city has three gates on each side, each named for a tribe, so every family of Israel has its own way in. To keep the number at twelve, Levi gets a gate and the two tribes descended from Joseph share one.

parts.label: "The LORD is there" (v. 35)
parts.note: The city is never called Jerusalem; its new name answers the earlier scene in this book where God's glory left the temple, and says God's presence has returned for good. Christians often read the city with twelve named gates in Revelation 21 as the fulfillment of this picture.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this vision describes a literal future land and temple in Israel, a symbolic picture of the church or the new creation, or an idealized hope given to exiles that was never meant as a blueprint.
think: Ezekiel's picture of a restored home ends not with walls or borders but with a presence; what do you think makes a place truly feel like home?
